item.title: মেক্সিকোর কাছে ১১টি ব্ল্যাক হক হেলিকপ্টার বিক্রির অনুমোদন যুক্তরাষ্ট্রের
item.description:
মেক্সিকোর কাছে ১১টি ইউএইচ-৬০এম ব্ল্যাক হক হেলিকপ্টার ও সংশ্লিষ্ট সরঞ্জাম বিক্রির সম্ভাব্য প্রস্তাব অনুমোদন করেছে যুক্তরাষ্ট্রের পররাষ্ট্র দফতর। এ বিক্রির আনুমানিক মূল্য ১০৭ কোটি ৫০ লাখ ডলার। শুক্রবার মার্কিন পররাষ্ট্র দফতর এ অনুমোদনের তথ্য জানিয়েছে।
মেক্সিকো সরকারের অনুরোধে প্রস্তাবিত এ বিক্রির আওতায় ১১টি হেলিকপ্টারের পাশাপাশি ২৭টি করে টি৭০০-জিই-৭০১ডি ইঞ্জিন, এমবেডেড গ্লোবাল পজিশনিং সিস্টেম ও ইনর্শিয়াল নেভিগেশন সিস্টেম এবং যোগাযোগের রেডিও সরঞ্জাম থাকবে। এ ছাড়া নাইট ভিশন গগলস, রাডার, মেশিনগান, উদ্ধারকাজের সরঞ্জাম, অতিরিক্ত যন্ত্রাংশ, প্রশিক্ষণ ও কারিগরি সহায়তাও প্যাকেজের অন্তর্ভুক্ত।
যুক্তরাষ্ট্রের পররাষ্ট্র দফতরের ভাষ্য, এই বিক্রি উত্তর আমেরিকায় রাজনৈতিক স্থিতিশীলতা ও অর্থনৈতিক অগ্রগতিতে ভূমিকা রাখা মিত্রদেশ মেক্সিকোর নিরাপত্তা জোরদারে সহায়তা করবে। পাশাপাশি দেশটির হেলিকপ্টার বহরের আধুনিকায়ন এবং বিভিন্ন ধরনের হেলিকপ্টারের ব্যবহার কমিয়ে ইউএইচ-৬০এম বহর সম্প্রসারণের মাধ্যমে কার্যকারিতা বাড়বে।
প্রস্তাবিত বিক্রি মাদকবিরোধী অভিযানে নিয়োজিত মেক্সিকোর বাহিনীর অভ্যন্তরীণ আকাশপথে পরিবহন সক্ষমতাও বাড়াবে। যুক্তরাষ্ট্রের পররাষ্ট্র দপ্তর বলেছে, এসব সরঞ্জাম ও সেবা মেক্সিকোর সশস্ত্র বাহিনীর ব্যবহারে যুক্ত করতে দেশটির কোনো অসুবিধা হবে না।
এ বিক্রির প্রধান ঠিকাদার যুক্তরাষ্ট্রের কানেকটিকাট অঙ্গরাজ্যের স্ট্র্যাটফোর্ডে অবস্থিত লকহিড মার্টিনের প্রতিষ্ঠান সিকোরস্কি। এ সম্ভাব্য বিক্রির সঙ্গে কোনও অফসেট চুক্তির প্রস্তাব সম্পর্কে এখন পর্যন্ত অবগত নয় যুক্তরাষ্ট্র সরকার। ক্রেতা ও ঠিকাদারের মধ্যে আলোচনার মাধ্যমে এ ধরনের চুক্তি নির্ধারিত হবে।
প্রস্তাবটি বাস্তবায়নে সরঞ্জাম প্রস্তুত করা, সরবরাহ, সিস্টেম পরীক্ষা, প্রশিক্ষণ এবং কারিগরি ও লজিস্টিক সহায়তার জন্য যুক্তরাষ্ট্র সরকারের বা ঠিকাদারি প্রতিষ্ঠানের অতিরিক্ত ১৫ জন প্রতিনিধিকে দীর্ঘ সময়ের জন্য মেক্সিকোতে যেতে হবে।
যুক্তরাষ্ট্রের পররাষ্ট্র দফতর জানিয়েছে, এ বিক্রির ফলে আঞ্চলিক সামরিক ভারসাম্যে মৌলিক কোনও পরিবর্তন হবে না। একই সঙ্গে যুক্তরাষ্ট্রের প্রতিরক্ষা প্রস্তুতির ওপরও এর কোনো বিরূপ প্রভাব পড়বে না।

item.title: Five priorities for Bangladesh ahead of COP31. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
For decades, Bangladesh has stood at the frontline of climate change. Rising sea levels, cyclones, floods, salinity intrusion, and heat stress have made the country one of the most climate-vulnerable nations in the world.
Yet Bangladesh has also become one of the world's most remarkable examples of climate adaptation and resilience-building.
Discussions on Bangladesh’s climate priorities ahead of COP31 took place during the 64th meeting of the Subsidiary Bodies (SB64) of the UNFCCC in Bonn from June 8-18. The Bangladesh delegation was led by the special assistant to the prime minister of the newly formed government. As in previous years, I had the opportunity to follow the climate discussions and negotiations at SB64 and engage in a dialogue with the special assistant on Bangladesh’s future climate strategies.
Our exchange highlighted an important opportunity: Moving beyond the narrative of vulnerability and positioning Bangladesh as a global leader in climate solutions.
Bangladesh’s experience, particularly in community-led adaptation and resilience-building, offers valuable lessons for the world. At the same time, the country has an opportunity to further strengthen its role in global climate action by combining adaptation leadership with innovation, collaboration, and strategic engagement.
Based on discussions and reflections from SB64, five priorities deserve particular attention as Bangladesh prepares for COP31.
Bangladesh's greatest climate success story is not found in international conference halls but in local communities.
Over the last decades, investments in cyclone preparedness, community-based disaster management, early warning systems, climate-resilient agriculture, and local adaptation initiatives have dramatically reduced climate-related mortality and strengthened resilience across vulnerable regions.
These achievements are increasingly recognized internationally as examples of successful adaptation in practice.
However, Bangladesh has not always been effective in translating these experiences into global influence. Stronger documentation, monitoring, and communication of adaptation outcomes are needed.
Robust data demonstrating how local adaptation initiatives reduce vulnerability, improve livelihoods, and strengthen resilience can help position Bangladesh as a global knowledge leader.
At a time when many countries are struggling to operationalize adaptation goals, Bangladesh possesses evidence and experience that the world urgently needs.
Adaptation will rightly remain Bangladesh's highest climate priority. Yet adaptation and mitigation should not be viewed as competing agendas.
The most successful climate investments increasingly deliver both emissions reductions and resilience benefits. Renewable energy systems can strengthen energy security during climate-related disruptions. Nature-based solutions such as mangrove restoration can simultaneously store carbon, reduce disaster risks, and protect livelihoods. Climate-smart agriculture can improve food security while reducing emissions.
By prioritizing mitigation projects that generate adaptation co-benefits, Bangladesh can strengthen its international position, attract additional financing, and demonstrate how developing countries can pursue integrated climate action.
Rather than choosing between adaptation and mitigation, Bangladesh can show how the two agendas reinforce one another.
Climate action is most effective when it is co-created. Bangladesh has a vibrant ecosystem of NGOs, community organizations, researchers, youth groups, social enterprises, and local governments working on climate issues. Yet these actors are not always fully integrated into national climate planning and implementation processes.
Future climate strategies should place greater emphasis on collaborative governance, participatory planning, and co-development. Citizens and local communities possess valuable knowledge about risks, vulnerabilities, and practical solutions. Their involvement improves both legitimacy and effectiveness.
International experience increasingly shows that climate transitions succeed when governments act not only as regulators but also as facilitators of collaboration between public, private, academic, and civil society actors.
As climate negotiations become increasingly complex, effective participation requires a diverse range of expertise.
Bangladesh has long been respected within the UNFCCC process, particularly on adaptation and climate justice. However, future negotiations will increasingly involve highly technical discussions around climate finance, carbon markets, technology transfer, loss and damage mechanisms, and implementation frameworks.
To maximize influence at COP31 and beyond, Bangladesh should continue expanding the diversity of expertise within its delegations. Alongside government officials, delegations can benefit from economists, scientists, legal experts, finance specialists, communication professionals, and experienced negotiators.
Strong climate diplomacy requires both technical knowledge and strategic negotiation skills.
Prepare for emerging carbon market opportunities
The operationalization of Article 6 of the Paris Agreement is creating new opportunities for international carbon trading and climate finance.
Many developing countries are now positioning themselves to benefit from emerging carbon markets through high-quality mitigation projects, nature-based solutions, and capacity-building initiatives. Bangladesh should actively prepare for this evolving landscape.
This requires investments in institutional capacity, transparent governance systems, project development expertise, monitoring frameworks, and stakeholder engagement. Universities, research institutions, private sector actors, and local communities all have important roles to play.
If approached strategically, carbon markets could become an additional source of climate finance while supporting sustainable development objectives.
A new chapter
Bangladesh has already demonstrated that climate vulnerability does not prevent climate leadership. The country's achievements in adaptation, disaster risk reduction, and resilience-building are recognized around the world.
The challenge now is to build on that foundation.
By showcasing community-led adaptation successes, integrating mitigation and resilience objectives, strengthening collaborative governance, enhancing negotiation capacity, and preparing for emerging climate finance opportunities, Bangladesh can help shape the global climate agenda rather than simply respond to it.
As the world prepares for COP31, Bangladesh has an opportunity to present itself not only as a country at risk from climate change, but as a country helping to define the solutions.
Dr Avit Bhowmik is a Climate Scientist and Associate Professor of Risk and Environmental Studies, Karlstad University, Sweden.

90 million displaced people at climate risk in Bangladesh, other countries: UNHCR
item.description:
REFUGEES-CLIMATE/UN

Nearly 90 million forcibly displaced people are living in countries increasingly exposed to climate-related droughts, floods and extreme heat, the UN refugee agency said on Friday, warning ahead of the COP31 climate summit that more funding is needed to help vulnerable communities adapt.

Nearly three-quarters of the world's forcibly displaced people are living in countries such as Afghanistan and Bangladesh that are exposed to severe climate-related risks, according to the report by the agency, known as UNHCR, published ahead of the UN Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Turkey. The findings show the overlap between conflict, displacement and climate change, the report said.

"Climate adaptation in fragile and displacement-affected areas is a matter of survival," said Anton Leis Garcia, UNHCR's assistant high commissioner for operations.

"We need climate financing to reach the communities where the needs are greatest," he said.

The report highlighted the experience of a Sudanese refugee who fled conflict in al-Fashir in June 2023 to the Farchana refugee settlement in eastern Chad. The refugee said she sometimes goes a week without finding safe water and must walk increasingly long distances for alternative sources as nearby seasonal riverbeds dry up amid intensifying heat.

Returns at risk

It also warned that climate change is making it harder for displaced people to return home sustainably.

In the first half of 2026, more than two-thirds of refugee returns were to countries highly exposed to climate hazards, placing them at risk of renewed displacement, the report said.

In Syria, where nearly 4 million displaced people have recently returned, people face worsening water scarcity and erratic rainfall, while flooding along the Euphrates River in May damaged homes and displaced thousands of people, the report said.

Across sub-Saharan Africa, one in three refugee settlements could experience at least 100 days of dangerous heat each year by 2050, threatening health and livelihoods, the report said. In some settlements in Ethiopia, including Helaweyn, dangerous heat could persist for more than 200 days a year, increasing the risks of heatstroke and premature death.

"Refugees often have limited access to cooling, water and reliable energy, making it harder to escape dangerous temperatures," the report said.

UNHCR also warned that a forecast supersized El Niño could worsen climate-related risks in many refugee-hosting countries and trigger further displacement.

In East Africa, severe flooding could displace up to 3 million people in Somalia, Kenya, South Sudan and Uganda by the end of this year, UNHCR said. In the Sahel, drought, flooding and conflict could intensify competition over scarce resources, while parts of Asia face heightened risks of droughts, floods and cyclones.

UNHCR called on governments and climate-finance institutions meeting at COP31 to increase funding for climate adaptation, highlighting that only about 10 per cent of climate finance reaches fragile or conflict-affected countries.

On Wednesday, a separate UN report found rich ​countries were falling well short of the $305 billion needed each year ‌to help developing nations adapt to climate change, even as extreme weather events become more frequent and severe.

item.description:
চীনের নৌবাহিনী এখন আর নিজেদের উপকূলীয় সীমানার মধ্যে সীমাবদ্ধ নেই। দক্ষিণ চীন সাগর থেকে শুরু করে জাপান ও তাইওয়ানের নিকটবর্তী জলসীমা পর্যন্ত এশিয়ার অন্যতম ব্যস্ত বাণিজ্যিক রুটগুলোতে প্রতিদিন প্রায় ১০০টি চীনা রণতরী চলাচল করছে। এছাড়া তারা পশ্চিম প্রশান্ত মহাসাগরের গভীরেও অভিযান পরিচালনা করছে এবং নিয়মিত এডেন উপসাগরে মোতায়েন থাকছে।
বেইজিংয়ের এই ক্রমবর্ধমান উপস্থিতি মার্কিন সামরিক পরিকল্পনাবিদদের জন্য চরম দুশ্চিন্তার কারণ হয়ে দাঁড়িয়েছে। চীনের বহরে এখন যুক্তরাষ্ট্রের চেয়েও বেশি যুদ্ধজাহাজ রয়েছে এবং এর সংখ্যা যেভাবে বাড়ছে, তার সঙ্গে পাল্লা দেওয়া ওয়াশিংটনের জন্য কঠিন হয়ে পড়ছে।
‘দ্য ওয়াল স্ট্রিট জার্নাল’-এ পর্যালোচিত সরকারি মার্কিন পরিসংখ্যান অনুযায়ী, চীনা নৌবাহিনীর এখন ৪০০টিরও বেশি রণতরী ও সাবমেরিন রয়েছে, যা জাহাজের সংখ্যার বিচারে মার্কিন নৌবহরের চেয়ে প্রায় ৩৫ শতাংশ বেশি। চীন বর্তমানে তিনটি বিমানবাহী রণতরী পরিচালনা করছে এবং চতুর্থটি নির্মাণের কাজ চলছে। পশ্চিমা বিশেষজ্ঞদের ধারণা, বেইজিংয়ের পরবর্তী বিমানবাহী রণতরীটি পরমাণুচালিত হতে পারে। এটি আধুনিক ইতিহাসে শান্তিকালীন সময়ে নৌবাহিনীর সর্ববৃহৎ সম্প্রসারণের অন্যতম ঘটনা।
নিরাপত্তা কর্মকর্তাদের মতে, তাইওয়ানের আশেপাশের জলসীমায় গড়ে প্রায় ছয়টি চীনা রণতরী অবস্থান করে। সামরিক মহড়ার সময় এই সংখ্যা অনেক বেড়ে যায়। অন্যদিকে দক্ষিণ চীন সাগরে এই উপস্থিতি প্রায় তিনগুণ বেশি, যেখানে ফিলিপাইন ও ভিয়েতনামের সঙ্গে বেইজিংয়ের আঞ্চলিক ভূখণ্ডের বিরোধ রয়েছে।
বেইজিংয়ের লক্ষ্য শুধু জাহাজের সংখ্যা বাড়ানো নয়; তারা নিজেদের উপকূলীয় জলসীমার ওপর পূর্ণ নিয়ন্ত্রণ প্রতিষ্ঠা করতে চায়, বিতর্কিত ভূখণ্ডের ওপর দাবি জোরদার করতে চায় এবং সম্ভাব্য সংঘাতের সময় মার্কিন বাহিনীকে হস্তক্ষেপ করা থেকে বিরত রাখতে চায়।

item.title: Holding the world accountable for the climate crisis. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
As world leaders assemble in Antalya, Türkiye, for the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), it is safe to say that the threat of climate change has long ceased to be an abstract projection and has become the most significant existential catastrophe for the entire planet.
This is particularly true for a nation such as ours. With global heat records continuously shattered and fragile coastal ecosystems buckling under systemic salinization and relentless riverine erosion, Bangladesh remains among the most affected nations - due to a crisis it had virtually no part in creating.
For decades, global climate summits have yielded ambitious rhetoric, bureaucratic inertia, and pledges devoid of enforcement. At COP31, our diplomatic delegation, and indeed others from the Global South, must enter negotiations not to petition for international goodwill, but to demand the immediate, enforceable execution of climate justice.
The bedrock of our negotiating must reflect the economic reality we face as a result of climate change. Bangladeshi leadership must resolutely hold the world’s primary industrial polluters, ie the Global North accountable.
At a time when Bangladesh is experiencing among its most challenging economic issues, the effects of climate change continue to destroy infrastructure, deplete agricultural yields, and cause mass human displacement. Yet, it has been sad to see international countermeasures remain egregiously disproportionate.
The global Loss and Damage Fund, which was secured after years of arduous diplomacy, remains severely undercapitalized, with current allocation frameworks failing to address the true scope of vulnerability.
At COP31, Bangladesh must lead the coalition of climate-vulnerable states in advocating for legally binding financial commitments and doing away with the unreliable paradigm of voluntary contributions that major economies routinely disregard.
Beyond loss and damage, we must also prioritize direct, grant-based adaptation capital. Bangladesh cannot continue to accept climate finance structured as debt-bearing loans, which serve only to exacerbate existing foreign reserve strains.
Global climate equity is not optional, and COP31 must mark a turning point where Bangladesh plays its part in compelling the international community to honour its obligations.

item.title: ভূমি নিবন্ধন কার্যক্রম ভূমি মন্ত্রণালয়ের অধীনে আনার সুপারিশ
item.description:
ভূমির নামজারি প্রক্রিয়া পুরোপুরি অটোমেশনের (স্বয়ংক্রিয়) আওতায় আনা এবং ভূমি নিবন্ধন কার্যক্রম ভূমি মন্ত্রণালয়ের অধীনে ন্যস্ত করার সুপারিশ করেছে ভূমি মন্ত্রণালয়–সম্পর্কিত সংসদীয় স্থায়ী কমিটি। সাবরেজিস্ট্রারদের দৌরাত্ম্য রোধ এবং হয়রানিমুক্ত ভূমিসেবা নিশ্চিত করার লক্ষ্যে এ সুপারিশ করা হয়েছে।

রোববার জাতীয় সংসদ ভবনে অনুষ্ঠিত কমিটির বৈঠকে ভূমি মন্ত্রণালয়কে এই সুপারিশ করা হয়। বৈঠক শেষে সংসদ সচিবালয়ের এক বিজ্ঞপ্তিতে এ তথ্য জানানো হয়েছে। বর্তমানে জমি নিবন্ধন বা রেজিস্ট্রেশনের কাজটি আইন মন্ত্রণালয়ের অধীনে হয়ে থাকে।

বিজ্ঞপ্তিতে বলা হয়েছে, বৈষম্য, অব্যবস্থাপনা ও দুর্নীতি দূর করে ন্যায়ভিত্তিক সমাজ প্রতিষ্ঠায় সরকার প্রতিশ্রুতিবদ্ধ। এ লক্ষ্য বাস্তবায়নে হয়রানিমুক্ত ও জনবান্ধব ভূমিসেবা নিশ্চিত করার সুপারিশ করা হয়। এ জন্য ভূমিসেবা জনগণের দোরগোড়ায় পৌঁছে দেওয়া, নামজারি প্রক্রিয়া স্বয়ংক্রিয় করা এবং সাবরেজিস্ট্রারদের দৌরাত্ম্য রোধে ভূমি রেজিস্ট্রেশন কার্যক্রম ভূমি মন্ত্রণালয়ের অধীনে আনার সুপারিশ করা হয়েছে।

জেলাওয়ারি অর্পিত সম্পত্তির পরিমাণ ও সম্ভাব্য মৌজা মূল্য নির্ধারণ এবং দীর্ঘদিন ধরে চলমান মামলা নিষ্পত্তির জন্য প্রয়োজনীয় পদক্ষেপ নেওয়ারও সুপারিশ করেছে কমিটি।

উপজেলা ও পৌর এলাকা এবং সিটি করপোরেশন এলাকার জন্য ভূমির প্রকৃত বাজারমূল্য নির্ধারণ, স্থাবর সম্পত্তির হস্তান্তর মূল্য বাজারদরের সঙ্গে যৌক্তিকীকরণসহ জমি হস্তান্তরসংক্রান্ত বিভিন্ন ফি ও গেইন ট্যাক্স যৌক্তিক পর্যায়ে নিয়ে আসার সুপারিশ করেছে কমিটি।

বিজ্ঞপ্তিতে আরও বলা হয়েছে, মাঠপর্যায়ে দুর্নীতি প্রতিরোধ, এসি ল্যান্ড, এলএ শাখা ও কানুনগো অফিসে সেবাগ্রহীতাদের হয়রানি বন্ধ এবং দালালমুক্ত ভূমিসেবা নিশ্চিত করতে প্রয়োজনীয় ব্যবস্থা নেওয়ার কথা বলা হয়েছে বৈঠকে।

একই জমির দলিল জামানত হিসেবে ব্যবহার করে একাধিক ব্যাংক থেকে ঋণ গ্রহণের মতো অনিয়ম প্রতিরোধে প্রয়োজনীয় ব্যবস্থা নিতে বলেছে কমিটি। বিদ্যমান প্রচলিত পদ্ধতির ভূমি প্রশাসন ব্যবস্থাপনাকে একটি সমন্বিত ডিজিটাল ভূমি প্রশাসন ব্যবস্থায় রূপান্তরিত করার সুপারিশও করা হয়।

কমিটির সভাপতি নাসের রহমানের সভাপতিত্বে সংসদ ভবনে এই বৈঠক অনুষ্ঠিত হয়। এতে কমিটির সদস্য ভূমিমন্ত্রী মিজানুর রহমান মিনু, জয়নাল আবদিন, সুলতানা আহমেদ, মো. মাহবুবুর রহমান বেলাল ও মুহাম্মদুল্লাহ অংশ নেন।

item.title: মুসলিম অভিবাসীদের মধ্যে ইহুদিবিদ্বেষ থাকলে জার্মানি ছাড়ার আহ্বান চ্যান্সেলর মের্ৎসের
item.description:
জার্মানির মুসলিম অভিবাসীদেরকেও দেশটিতে হওয়া হলোকাস্ট বা ইহুদি গণহত্যার ঐতিহাসিক দায়দায়িত্ব স্বীকার করতে হবে। এই দায়িত্ব যাঁরা স্বীকার করবেন না, তাঁদের জার্মানি ছেড়ে যেতে হবে বলে মন্তব্য করেছেন দেশটির চ্যান্সেলর ফ্রিডরিখ মের্ৎস।

জার্মানির রাজধানী বার্লিনে গত শুক্রবার ইহুদি ক্রীড়াবিদদের এক সংবর্ধনা অনুষ্ঠানে মের্ৎস এ কথা বলেন। জার্মান প্রেস এজেন্সি (ডিপিএ) সূত্রে এ খবর জানিয়েছে স্থানীয় সংবাদমাধ্যম বার্লিনার জাইটুং। বার্লিনে চ্যান্সেলরের কার্যালয়ে ২০২৬ সালের ‘মাকাবিয়া’ ক্রীড়া প্রতিযোগিতায় পদকজয়ীদের সম্মানে এ অনুষ্ঠানের আয়োজন করা হয়। ইসরায়েলে প্রতি চার বছর পরপর অনুষ্ঠিত হয় ইহুদিদের এই আন্তর্জাতিক ক্রীড়া প্রতিযোগিতা। এটি ‘ইহুদি অলিম্পিক’ নামেও পরিচিত।

অনুষ্ঠানে একজন বাস্কেটবল প্রশিক্ষক মের্ৎসকে বলেন, তাঁর দলের ইহুদি ক্রীড়াবিদেরা জার্মানির রাস্তায় ডেভিডের তারকা চিহ্নসংবলিত লাল মাকাবি ট্রেনিং জ্যাকেট পরে বের হতে ভয় পান। কারণ, এ কারণে তাঁদের ওপর হামলা হতে পারে বলে আশঙ্কা রয়েছে।

এর জবাবে মের্ৎস জার্মানির সাবেক রাষ্ট্রপতি রিশার্ড ফন ভাইৎসেকারের ১৯৮৫ সালে দেশটির সংসদে দেওয়া একটি ঐতিহাসিক ভাষণের প্রসঙ্গ তোলেন। দ্বিতীয় বিশ্বযুদ্ধের অবসানের ৪০ বছর পূর্তি উপলক্ষে দেওয়া ওই ভাষণে নাৎসি বাহিনীর অপরাধ এবং লাখ লাখ ইহুদিকে পরিকল্পিতভাবে হত্যার দায় ও দায়িত্বের কথা স্মরণ করিয়ে দিয়েছিলেন ভাইৎসেকার।

১৯৮৫ সালের ৮ মে দেওয়া ওই ভাষণে ভাইৎসেকার বলেছিলেন, ‘অতীতে যা ঘটেছিল, তার জন্য তরুণেরা দায়ী নয়; কিন্তু ইতিহাসে সেই ঘটনার পরিণতি কী হবে, তার জন্য তারা দায়ী।’

মের্ৎস বলেন, ভাইৎসেকারের এই কথাগুলো তাঁর কাছে পাথরে খোদাই করা সত্যের মতো অটল। এই দায়িত্ব জার্মানির সমগ্র সমাজের জন্য প্রযোজ্য। বর্তমান পরিস্থিতির কথা উল্লেখ করে তিনি আরও বলেন, ‘ইসলামি দেশগুলো থেকে যাঁরা জার্মানিতে আসেন, তাঁদের ক্ষেত্রেও আমাদের দেশের এই ঐতিহাসিক দায়িত্ব ঠিক একইভাবে প্রযোজ্য। আর কেউ যদি এই দায়িত্ব মেনে না চলেন, তাহলে তাঁকে আমাদের দেশ ছেড়ে চলে যেতে হবে।’

মুসলিম অভিবাসীদের একাংশের বিরুদ্ধে ইহুদিবিদ্বেষমূলক কর্মকাণ্ডের অভিযোগের প্রসঙ্গেই মের্ৎস এ মন্তব্য করেন।

item.title: Public university admission applications in January, exams to begin in February: UGC Chairman
item.description:
Applications for first-year undergraduate (honours) admission at the country’s public universities will begin in January next year, while admission tests are planned for February.

The decision was made at a meeting with vice-chancellors of public universities at the University Grants Commission (UGC) on Monday to discuss the schedule and other related matters for the 2026–27 academic year.

The meeting discussed students’ interests, admission test schedules, publication of results of the Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) supplementary examinations and coordination of the admission process.

It was also decided that universities will set and announce their examination dates through mutual coordination.

UGC Chairman Professor Mamun Ahmed shared the decisions at a press conference after the meeting.

The UGC chairman said the number of students who passed this year’s HSC and equivalent examinations was lower than last year. More than 700,000 students passed in 2025, while the figure was slightly over 600,000 in 2026.

He said answer scripts had been evaluated properly this year, as a result of which many students did not achieve their expected results. The authorities are arranging re-evaluation of answer scripts and supplementary examinations for these students.

The government is working towards publishing the results of the re-evaluation and supplementary examinations by 31 December. The public university admission process will begin after that, he said.

Students who pass the HSC supplementary examinations or obtain revised results following re-evaluation will be eligible to sit for university admission tests.

Mamun Ahmed said vice-chancellors had been asked to take the holy month of Ramadan into consideration when setting admission test schedules.

He also urged universities that have already announced their admission test dates to reconsider their schedules in the national interest and for the convenience of students.

item.title: NCP wants to keep Jamaat ‘in line’ while remaining in alliance
item.description:
The National Citizen Party (NCP), a partner in the same alliance, is dissatisfied with some of Jamaat-e-Islami’s recent political positions. The party’s policymakers believe Jamaat has become too accommodating towards the government in its role as an opposition party.

Against this backdrop, NCP has adopted a strategy of putting pressure on Jamaat still remaining part of the 11-party alliance. At the same time, the party wants to assert its own distinct political identity as well.

Prothom Alo learned of this stance after speaking to seven members of NCP’s political council, its highest policymaking body.

The growing distance between the two parties has come into focus through senior NCP leaders’ public criticism of Jamaat’s role in the recent by-election in Thakurgaon-1 and NCP’s limited participation in the 11-party alliance’s Khulna divisional long march on 31 October. NCP leaders, however, have said they do not want to leave the alliance.

NCP has adopted a strategy of putting pressure on Jamaat still remaining part of the 11-party alliance. At the same time, the party wants to assert its own distinct political identity as well.

In September, almost all the senior leaders of NCP, including convener Nahid Islam and member secretary Akhtar Hossain, took part in person in the first two long marches organised by the Jamaat-led 11-party alliance.

However, NCP’s participation in the alliance’s Khulna divisional long march on 31 October was merely ‘symbolic’. The party’s two top leaders did not attend.

Instead, on the day before the Khulna long march, the NCP organised a mass protest programme in the capital’s Shahbagh area. The party also conducted a week-long publicity campaign around the programme. During that campaign, NCP leaders made no mention of the long march, although they had been quite vocal ahead of the previous two marches.

These developments surrounding the 31 October long march have brought renewed attention to the ‘distance’ between the NCP and its alliance partner, Jamaat.

NCP policymakers say recent developments have led them to believe that Jamaat is forgetting its role as a genuine opposition party and becoming too accommodating towards the government. The NCP wants to put pressure on Jamaat to prevent it from becoming overly ‘effusive’ towards the government or the ruling party.

A senior NCP leader said they wanted to keep Jamaat ‘in line’ by criticising it while remaining in the 11-party alliance. This would also help counter what the leader described as ‘malicious propaganda’ claiming that the NCP was being absorbed into Jamaat. It would therefore help the party preserve its distinct identity.

NCP policymakers say recent developments have led them to believe that Jamaat is forgetting its role as a genuine opposition party and becoming too accommodating towards the government. NCP wants to put pressure on Jamaat to prevent it from becoming overly ‘effusive’ towards the government or the ruling party.

Public criticism over the Thakurgaon by-election

Voting in the by-election for the Thakurgaon-1 constituency took place on 29 October. Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) candidate Mirza Faisal Amin (brother of President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir) was unofficially declared elected after securing 227,917 votes.

His closest rival, Jamaat candidate Delawar Hossain, received 96,513 votes. The gap between the winning and losing candidates was 131,404 votes.

However, even before the results were announced, Jamaat called a protest, alleging irregularities, ballot stuffing and that polling agents had been beaten and forced out of polling stations.

Mirza Faisal visits defeated Jamaat candidate’s home with bouquet; Delwar says, ‘Best of luck’

But the following day, around noon, the winning BNP candidate visited the Jamaat candidate’s home with a bouquet of flowers. The two embraced and exchanged sweets. They also expressed their resolve to work together for the development of the area.

While this was happening in Thakurgaon, the picture in Dhaka was quite different. On the afternoon of 30 October, Jamaat Secretary General Mia Golam Porwar held a press conference at the party’s central office in Moghbazar in the capital.

He said ballot papers had been stamped in advance, fake votes cast and polling agents driven out of polling stations during the Thakurgaon-1 by-election.

If the Election Commission secretary and chief denied the irregularities, it would mean that the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and the EC secretary had colluded with those responsible. They had failed to do justice to their constitutional positions, he added.

NCP leaders publicly criticised what they described as Jamaat’s ‘double standards’. The first to speak out was former adviser to the interim government and NCP Senior Joint Member Secretary Asif Mahmud Shojib Bhuyain. Hasnat Abdullah, a member of parliament and NCP senior joint convener, also criticised the party.

Hasnat Abdullah We cannot claim from Dhaka that there was vote rigging and then accept the results. That is not how an opposition party should act. We cannot say there was vote rigging and then go and exchange sweets. That is not what opposition means.

Speaking at a mass protest in Shahbagh on the afternoon of 30 October, Asif Mahmud said, “There was a by-election in Thakurgaon. From the morning, we saw presiding officers in various places stamping ballot papers in advance, and they were caught doing so.”

“What is deeply disappointing is that we see the candidate from the ruling party and the opposition candidate exchanging sweets with each other. Our democracy is going through a period of severe crisis and distress,” he added.

Hasnat Abdullah also criticised Jamaat’s role in the Thakurgaon by-election while attending a roadside rally in Jashore as an NCP representative during the Khulna long march.

Although he did not name any party, Hasnat said, “We cannot claim from Dhaka that there was vote rigging and then accept the results. That is not how an opposition party should act. We cannot say there was vote rigging and then go and exchange sweets. That is not what opposition means.”

Tensions between NCP leadership and Samanta stretched back months

Following these public remarks by Asif Mahmud and Hasnat Abdullah, discussion about the ‘distance’ between Jamaat and NCP has intensified in political circles. Over the past few days, supporters of the two parties have also made posts countering eac other on Facebook.

Various Facebook accounts supporting Jamaat have claimed that the NCP wants Jamaat’s backing in at least one of the two Dhaka city corporation elections in the upcoming local government polls. According to these accounts, the NCP is trying to put pressure on Jamaat in order to secure that support.

However, NCP Joint Convener Ariful Islam Adeeb told Prothom Alo, “Some of Jamaat’s political positions are creating distrust among the public. For example, it makes very strong statements on the streets but takes the opposite position in parliament, and gives the government its blank support during labour movements.”

“That is why we have taken a separate position. Our stance is essentially political. There is no question of bargaining here,” he added.

NCP Joint Convener Sarwar TusherBreaking up the alliance or creating a rift within it, is part of the government’s agenda. We are not falling into that trap.

Behind the ‘rift’

Prothom Alo spoke to seven members of NCP’s political council, the party’s highest policymaking body, to understand the reasons behind the apparent ‘rift’ between the NCP and Jamaat.

They said NCP has come to feel that Jamaat did not want to put pressure on the government during its first two years in office. Instead, it wanted to proceed somewhat cautiously and take things slowly.

The NCP, however, does not agree with this approach. It is therefore maintaining its own distinct tone, which is at times creating distance between the two parties, they said.

One member of NCP’s political council said, “When Jamaat tries to put pressure on the government over various issues and then holds formal or informal discussions with it, the party becomes somewhat accommodating. This has an impact on the other parties in the opposition alliance.”

“When Jamaat puts pressure on the government, the other parties also adopt the same stance. But when it suddenly becomes accommodating, the other parties are left in an awkward position. This is what we are trying to address,” added the NCP leader.

An NCP policymaker said that whenever the 11-party alliance takes a political position, it should be based on discussions involving all the parties in the alliance.

Speaking to Prothom Alo, he said that when Jamaat suddenly adopts a more accommodating stance towards the BNP without informing the other parties, it creates an awkward situation. If being accommodating towards the government is part of a strategy, the other alliance partners should also be informed.

Leaders of the party said NCP has come to feel that Jamaat did not want to put pressure on the government during its first two years in office. Instead, it wanted to proceed somewhat cautiously and take things slowly.

The leader also cited several reasons behind this perception of NCP. These included Jamaat Ameer and opposition leader Shafiqur Rahman’s demand for a special committee on constitutional reform during the first session of the current parliament on 31 March. He had proposed that the committee have equal numbers of members from the ruling and opposition parties.

NCP was also uncomfortable with Shafiqur Rahman’s remarks in parliament on 7 September that the ongoing energy crisis was not caused by the current government. The party also believes that Jamaat’s initial position on the recent labour protests was not appropriate.

NCP leaders said they wanted to keep pressure on Jamaat to ensure that it properly fulfils its role as an opposition party. They said NCP wanted to pursue genuine opposition politics. They also claimed that Jamaat had changed its earlier positions on several issues as a result of pressure from the NCP.

Despite seeking to put pressure on Jamaat, NCP has no intention of leaving the 11-party alliance. On this, the party’s Joint Convener Sarwar Tusher told Prothom Alo, “Breaking up the alliance or creating a rift within it, is part of the government’s agenda. We are not falling into that trap.”

item.title: PM leaves tomorrow for COP31 summit in Turkiye
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will leave here tomorrow for Türkiye to attend the COP31 World Leaders' Summit, where he will address a plenary session and hold bilateral meetings on the sidelines.

The summit is scheduled to take place in Antalya on 11-12 November, with the Prime Minister set to deliver Bangladesh's statement at a plenary session on 12 November.

COP, officially known as the Conference of the Parties, is the annual United Nations climate summit where countries discuss collective action to address climate change.

Newly appointed Foreign Secretary Salahuddin Noman Chowdhury briefed reporters on preparations for the visit at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs today.

The Prime Minister will undertake the official visit from 10 to 12 November to lead the Bangladesh delegation.

His spouse Zubaida Rahman, the Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, the two state ministers for foreign affairs, the Prime Minister's Special Assistant on Environment, Forest and Climate Change, relevant government officials, a media team and other distinguished individuals will accompany him.

The foreign secretary said arrangements for the Prime Minister's engagements on the sidelines of the summit were still being finalised.

Bilateral meetings are being arranged with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, the Australian Prime Minister, the President of Uzbekistan and the British Foreign Secretary.

PM Tarique Rahman’s three-country tour planned for October, November

A meeting with the Administrator of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) is also being explored.

The meetings are expected to cover strengthening bilateral relations, expanding trade and investment, cooperation in addressing climate change and other matters of mutual interest.

Chowdhury expressed the hope that these engagements would create new opportunities to advance Bangladesh's economic and geopolitical interests.

Responding to a question about a possible courtesy meeting between the Prime Minister and the Turkish President, he said there was a possibility of such an engagement, during which overall cooperation between the two countries would be discussed.

The two sides could discuss the broader relationship, but specific project arrangements were unlikely to be settled during a courtesy meeting on the sidelines of a multilateral conference, he said.

Asked about Turkish company Çelebi’s interest in providing ground handling services at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport's third terminal as a partner of Biman Bangladesh Airlines under the Japanese consortium, he said detailed discussions on that particular proposal were unlikely during such a meeting.

On compensation for climate-related losses and damage, Chowdhury said Bangladesh presents estimates of the damage it has suffered before international forums to raise awareness and mobilise cooperation.

He said there were various estimates of Bangladesh's climate-related losses, which the country highlights in global discussions.

90 million displaced people at climate risk in Bangladesh, other countries: UNHCR

Presenting these concerns internationally helps create awareness about Bangladesh's situation and works in the country's favour, he added.

Asked how much compensation Bangladesh had secured through the COP process, the foreign secretary said the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change would be able to provide the relevant information.

He also distinguished compensation from the broader assistance and cooperation Bangladesh receives through presenting its position in international forums.

In his plenary address, the Prime Minister will outline Bangladesh's position and expectations on climate justice, the historical responsibility of developed countries, climate finance, adaptation, addressing loss and damage, and climate-resilient sustainable development.

Chowdhury said Bangladesh contributes only 0.05 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet remains among the countries most vulnerable to the adverse impacts of climate change.

Against this backdrop, securing climate justice is one of Bangladesh's foremost priorities, he said.

Other priorities include adaptation finance, addressing loss and damage, and ensuring the effective implementation of developed countries' climate finance commitments.

At the summit, Bangladesh will highlight its achievements in climate resilience and share its experience in addressing climate impacts across South Asia and the wider Asian region.

Bangladesh has also taken an initiative to establish a jute pavilion in the conference's Green Zone to showcase jute's diverse uses, environmentally friendly characteristics and potential as an alternative to plastic.

PM urges global leaders to turn climate pledges into action

A joint declaration between Bangladesh and Turkiye on the use and promotion of jute and jute products is also envisaged during the conference, the foreign secretary said.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs will organise two side events in the Blue Zone on 12 and 13 November.

One will focus on gender-based vulnerability in Bangladesh resulting from the adverse impacts of climate change, while the other will address the challenges of promoting environmentally friendly, biodegradable and zero-waste jute products.

The events will draw international attention to the particular risks women face because of climate change and the scope for expanding the use of jute products as alternatives to synthetic polymer-based products.

Chowdhury said Trkiye is presiding over this year's conference, while Australia is co-chairing the formal climate negotiation process.

He said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs had coordinated with the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change and other relevant ministries and agencies to prepare for Bangladesh's participation.

The country's positions and priorities were determined through inter-ministerial discussions and consultations with stakeholders, he added.

The foreign secretary expressed the hope that Bangladesh's participation under the Prime Minister's leadership would strengthen its position in international climate diplomacy and provide an opportunity to showcase its efforts and achievements in building climate resilience.

Additional Foreign Secretary (Public Diplomacy and Other Priority Matters) AKM Shahidul Karim and senior ministry officials were present at the briefing.

Public university admission tests to begin in February
item.description:
First-year admission tests at public universities for the 2026-27 academic session are expected to begin in February next year, with applications opening in January.
University Grants Commission (UGC) Chairman Professor Dr Mamun Ahmed announced the plan at a press briefing on Monday following a meeting with public university vice-chancellors at the UGC headquarters.
He said universities had agreed to coordinate their admission test schedules to avoid clashes and allow students to sit for tests at multiple institutions.
The decision comes as the number of students who passed this year's Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations fell to slightly over 600,000, down from more than 700,000 last year.
Mamun said answer scripts were being re-evaluated and supplementary examinations arranged for students who failed to achieve their expected results. The government aims to publish the results of both by December 31.
Students who pass the re-evaluation or supplementary examinations will also be eligible for university admission tests, he added.
The UGC chairman said vice-chancellors had been asked to consider Ramadan when setting admission test dates. Universities that have already announced their schedules have also been urged to reconsider them to avoid clashes.
The meeting also discussed forming a central coordination committee comprising representatives from the UGC, the Ministry of Education and universities to oversee admission schedules throughout the year.
On admission test formats, Mamun said universities would retain the multiple-choice question (MCQ) system for the current academic session. However, they are considering introducing subject-based and analytical questions alongside MCQs from the next session to assess students' subject knowledge, analytical skills and problem-solving abilities.
Vice-chancellors were also asked to consider GPA requirements in determining admission test eligibility, taking into account this year's HSC results and available seats.
Mamun said universities had been urged to ensure that the delayed admission tests did not disrupt regular academic activities, adding that the UGC would provide necessary support.
Bangladesh currently has around 180 public and private universities. Public universities offer approximately 63,000 first-year seats, while institutions affiliated with the National University, Islamic Arabic University and other public universities have more than one million seats combined. Private universities offer more than 400,000 seats.
He stressed that the coordination initiative would respect university autonomy, with institutions retaining authority over their admission processes under their respective laws and regulations.

item.title: PM Tarique to leave for Türkiye Tuesday to attend COP31 summit
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will leave Dhaka on Tuesday for an official visit to Türkiye to attend the World Leaders’ Summit of COP31, scheduled to be held in Antalya on November 11-12.
The prime minister is scheduled to address a plenary session on November 12 and hold several bilateral meetings with world leaders on the sidelines of the summit.
Newly appointed Foreign Secretary Salahuddin Noman Chowdhury briefed reporters about the visit at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Sunday.
Bangladesh is looking to arrange bilateral meetings with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, the Australian prime minister, the president of Uzbekistan and the British foreign secretary.
Additional Foreign Secretary (Public Diplomacy and Other Priority Matters) AKM Shahidul Karim and senior ministry officials were also present.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam recently said Bangladesh would urge developed countries to provide climate finance in the form of grants rather than loans and take responsibility for their contribution to global carbon emissions at the upcoming COP31.
COP, officially known as the Conference of the Parties, is the annual United Nations climate summit.
Bangladesh will highlight its achievements in climate resilience and share its experience in addressing the impacts of climate change across South Asia and the wider Asian region.
At the same time, the country will draw attention to the support it needs to tackle future climate challenges, particularly the importance of ensuring that climate finance comes in the form of grants rather than loans.
Bangladesh will also press major carbon-emitting countries to take responsibility for their emissions and ensure accountability in global climate negotiations.
"Although Bangladesh's contribution to global carbon emissions is almost negligible, we are ultimately among those suffering the consequences," Shama Obaed said recently.
The government will also showcase the initiatives taken by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman over the past six months to address climate change and improve the environment.
These include canal excavation, tree plantation drives and a stronger focus on solar power and renewable energy, all of which contribute to climate change mitigation and environmental protection.
An inter-ministerial coordination meeting chaired by State Minister Shama last month reviewed Bangladesh's preparations for the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31).
The meeting discussed various aspects of the preparations, including the Prime Minister's participation in the high-level segment of the summit.
It also reviewed Bangladesh's priorities and concerns, possible bilateral engagements and seminars to be organised at the country's pavilions in the Blue and Green Zones on the sidelines of COP31.

item.title: 34 platoons of BGB deployed in industrial areas of Dhaka, Gazipur, Narayanganj
item.description:
A total of 34 platoons of the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) have been deployed in key industrial areas of Dhaka, Gazipur and Narayanganj to ensure security, maintain law and order and prevent any untoward incidents amid ongoing worker unrest.
The BGB Media Department disclosed the information on Monday.
The deployed personnel are performing duties at various key locations, including Savar, Ashulia and Mirpur in Dhaka; Shibu Market, Jalkuri, BSCIC Industrial Estate, Chashara, Kanchpur and Shimrail in Narayanganj; and Chandra, Kaliakair, Palli Bidyut, Mouchak, Ambag Kata, Naojor, Bhogra Bypass, Gacha and Salna in Gazipur.
The BGB headquarters' monitoring cell is continuing technology-based surveillance to closely monitor the overall situation in industrial areas and coordinate the activities of personnel deployed on the ground.
Live footage obtained through drones, body-worn cameras and improvised devices is being monitored round the clock.
BGB personnel are performing their duties on high alert in coordination with the local administration and police.
The force is also maintaining necessary preparations and operations to address any unforeseen situation and maintain peace and order in industrial areas.

item.title: মহেশখালীতে হচ্ছে আরও ৩ এলএনজি টার্মিনাল: মুখ্য সচিব
item.description:
প্রধানমন্ত্রীর মুখ্য সচিব এ বি এম আব্দুস সাত্তার বলেছেন, কক্সবাজারের মহেশখালীতে আরও তিনটি এলএনজি টার্মিনাল হচ্ছে।
রবিবার (৮ নভেম্বর) মহেশখালী সমন্বিত উন্নয়ন কর্তৃপক্ষের অধীন মাতারবাড়ীতে নির্মাণাধীন গভীর সমুদ্র বন্দর কয়লানির্ভর বিদ্যুৎ কেন্দ্র, ধলঘাটা মাতারবাড়ী রাজঘাট এলাকা পরিদর্শন শেষে ব্রিফিংয়ে এ কথা বলেন তিনি।
মুখ্য সচিব বলেন, দেশের জ্বালানি সংকট নিরসনের লক্ষ্যে সরকার মহেশখালী সমুদ্র উপকূলে একটি এবং মহেশখালীর মাতারবাড়ীতে ল্যান্ড বেইজ আরও দুটি এলএনজি টার্মিনাল স্থাপন করবে। আগামী দুই বছরে এলএনজি টার্মিনালের কার্যক্রম দৃশ্যমান হবে।
তিনি বলেন, মাতারবাড়ীতে বিভিন্ন প্রকল্পে ক্ষতিগ্রস্তদের পুনর্বাসন করা হবে। পাশাপাশি তাদের মধ্যে উপযুক্তদের চাকরিসহ আরও নানা সুযোগ-সুবিধা দেওয়া হবে।
তিনি বলেন, বর্তমান সরকারের আমলে মাতারবাড়ীতে আরও উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প হবে এবং গভীর সমুদ্র বন্দরের কাজ শেষ হলে দেশের আমূল পরিবর্তন আসবে।
প্রধানমন্ত্রীর মুখ্য সচিব বলেন, বিগত সরকারের আমলে নতজানু পররাষ্ট্র নীতির কারণে এই প্রকল্পগুলো আলোর মুখ দেখেনি। কিন্তু বর্তমান সরকার দ্রুত সময়ের মধ্যে প্রকল্পের কাজ শেষ করবেন এবং সেই লক্ষ্যেই কাজ চলছে।
এ সময় প্রধানমন্ত্রীর বিশেষ সহকারী বিজন কান্তি সরকার, স্থানীয় সংসদ সদস্য আলমগীর মোহাম্মদ মাহফুজ উল্লাহ ফরিদসহ প্রকল্পের ঊর্ধ্বতন কর্মকর্তারা উপস্থিত ছিলেন।

item.title: EC plans to hold first-phase elections in 1,000 UPs on 21 January
item.description:
The Election Commission (EC) plans to hold elections in around 1,000 union parishads (UPs) in the first phase on 21 January next year, as part of a five-phase election programme.

EC Senior Secretary Akhtar Ahmed disclosed the plan while speaking to journalists at the Election Commission Bhaban in Agargaon today.

He said the second phase is likely to be held on 4 February, while the third, fourth and fifth phases are scheduled for 29 April, 13 May and 27 May, respectively.

The schedule has been planned considering Ramadan, the Secondary School Certificate (SSC) examinations and weather conditions, particularly in coastal areas.

According to the EC, approximately 1,000 UPs will go to polls in the first phase. The terms of around 4,300 union parishads have already expired, and elections to these local government bodies will be completed by 27 May, 2027.

The EC is considering UPs whose terms have expired or are due to expire within the election schedule period. It has almost completed preparations for the first phase, while the lists of UPs for the first and second phases are expected to be finalised by Thursday.

Akhtar Ahmed said elections in all union parishads of an upazila would be held simultaneously if their terms had expired or they had become eligible for elections.

Some UP elections remain pending due to court cases. However, these could be included if final court verdicts are delivered before the final list is published.

He said preparations for the elections were progressing, including checking election materials and arranging the printing of ballot papers for chairman, general member and reserved women member posts.

The EC has also held discussions with the Bangladesh Government Press and Security Printing Press regarding ballot printing.

The decision to hold the UP elections in five phases was taken at a Commission meeting on 12 October.

Election Commissioner Brigadier General (Retd) Abul Fazal Md Sanaullah earlier confirmed the five-phase schedule and said all elections would be completed by 27 May next year.

item.title: Anyone saying ‘December is at the door’ has no connection with Bangladesh: Adviser Titumir
item.description:
Those who are talking about the Awami League’s return next December have no connection with Bangladesh, said Professor Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, the Prime Minister’s Adviser on Finance and Planning.

He said there was currently no one capable of reviving the Awami League, unlike the situation after 1975, when efforts were made to revive the party.

Professor Titumir described the “ousting of the Awami League” by the people of Bangladesh in 2024 as a victory for the country.

He made the remarks as the chief guest at a discussion titled “The Famine of 1974: Post-Independence Economic Crisis”, held at the Monsoon Theatre Hall of the July Mass Uprising Memorial Museum on Sunday afternoon.

The discussion was the fifth instalment of the museum’s Democratic Journey Seminar Series.

“If anyone says that ‘December is knocking at the door’, it should be understood that they have no connection with the soil, grass or water of Bangladesh,” Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir said.

Titumir, a professor in the Department of Development Studies at Dhaka University, said the 1974 famine could not be explained solely by food shortages or failures in the market system. Rather, it was also rooted in the state’s estrangement from the people, a crisis of political legitimacy and the role of violence.

The prime minister’s adviser pointed to continuities between the systems of governance from 1972 to 1975 and the Awami League government’s rule from 2009 to 2024.

He said both periods were characterised by governments becoming detached from people’s aspirations and attempting to retain power through patronage and violence.

Titumir said similar tendencies were evident during both 1971–75 and 2009–24, including the suppression of opposition, abuse of state power and the use of violence to remain in office.

Rashe Al Mahmud Titumir said three theories are generally put forward to explain the 1974 famine. These concern a decline in overall food availability, people’s lack of purchasing power or access to food, and the absence of a social contract to prevent famine. The influence of international food aid and Cold War geopolitics is also cited.

However, he argued that these explanations fail to adequately address the crisis in the relationship between the state and its people.

According to the incumbent PM’s adviser, people’s aspirations were not reflected in the way the country was governed after independence. A disconnect developed between the people and those in power. In these circumstances, a system of patronage emerged as a means of retaining power, extending from rural areas to the centre. The influence of this patronage system was also evident in “rationing” and food distribution.

Titumir said similar tendencies were evident during both 1971–75 and 2009–24, including the suppression of opposition, abuse of state power and the use of violence to remain in office.

He also pointed to similarities in food prices during the two periods. While international rice prices fell, prices in the Bangladeshi market rose, he said. The international price of rice stood at US$147 per tonne in 1972 before rising to $542 in 1974. He noted that domestic prices in Bangladesh were higher than those in the international market during the same period.

The prime minister’s adviser further said that when the state becomes alienated from the people and resorts to violence to retain power, conditions conducive to famine and plunder emerge. Therefore, any discussion of the 1974 famine must consider not only economic statistics but also state violence and loss of life during that period.

Describing the 2024 mass uprising as a victory for the people, Titumir said Bangladeshis had repeatedly asserted their sovereignty. He said the people had played a role in establishing their rights in 1971, 1975, 1990 and 2024.

However, he stressed that making this victory sustainable required effective state institutions. Highlighting the role of the Jatiya Sangsad (national parliament), he said the state must retain the exclusive authority to exercise legitimate “violence”, but that authority must remain accountable.

An effective parliament was essential for this purpose, he said. Article 7 of the Constitution recognises the sovereignty of the people, and parliament is the institution through which this principle must be upheld. The challenges of state-building cannot be addressed through street movements without making parliament effective, he added.

The prime minister’s adviser further said that when the state becomes alienated from the people and resorts to violence to retain power, conditions conducive to famine and plunder emerge. Therefore, any discussion of the 1974 famine must consider not only economic statistics but also state violence and loss of life during that period.

The seminar was chaired by Ehsan Mahmud, director-general of the July Mass Uprising Memorial Museum. Writer and treasurer of the Panam Institute Asif Iqbal, and economist and researcher Nahian bin Khaled, also spoke at the event.

item.title: Bangladesh takes climate justice demand to COP31
item.description:
Bangladesh will press for increased grant-based climate finance, stronger global commitments on adaptation and greater accountability from major polluters at the upcoming COP31 climate summit, seeking international support to tackle worsening climate impacts without adding to the country’s debt burden.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is scheduled to attend the two-day World Leaders’ Summit on November 11–12, where he is expected to present Bangladesh’s priorities on climate justice, international financial commitments and support for implementing national climate plans.
The 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) will take place in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20. It is expected to bring together world leaders, climate negotiators, development partners, civil society representatives and international organizations.
Bangladesh’s central message is that the countries bearing the greatest climate risks, despite contributing relatively little to global emissions, should not have to take on more debt to protect their people.
Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo outlined the country’s negotiating priorities at a press conference at the Secretariat in Dhaka on Thursday.
Special Assistant to the Prime Minister for Environment and Climate Change Dr Saimum Parvez, Acting Secretary of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change Dr Fahmida Khanam, Additional Secretary Navid Saifullah and Bangladesh Climate Change Trust Managing Director Kazi Rawnaqul Islam were also present.
Mintoo said Bangladesh would prioritize climate justice, protection of vulnerable communities and international financial and technological support for implementing its climate commitments. He emphasized the need for adequate, predictable and accessible climate finance, primarily in the form of grants, alongside stronger support for adaptation and addressing loss and damage.
Separately, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said on Monday that Bangladesh would urge developed countries to provide climate finance as grants rather than loans and take responsibility for their contribution to global carbon emissions. Her remarks reinforce Dhaka’s position that climate finance should reflect the historical responsibility of major emitters and the financial needs of vulnerable developing countries.
Bangladesh has prepared a national position paper through consultations with relevant ministries, government agencies and climate experts. It will also coordinate its negotiating position with the Least Developed Countries (LDC) Group, the Group of 77 and China, and other climate-vulnerable countries.
Climate finance is expected to be one of Bangladesh’s principal priorities at COP31, with Dhaka seeking stronger implementation of commitments made by developed countries under international climate agreements. The country will call for new, additional, predictable and accessible resources to support adaptation, resilience-building and the implementation of national climate plans.
A key demand will be that assistance for climate-vulnerable developing countries should come primarily through grants instead of loans. Bangladesh argues that loan-based climate assistance can increase public debt and place an additional financial burden on countries already dealing with the economic consequences of climate change.
The government will also press for simpler application and approval procedures for international climate funds. Lengthy processes and complex administrative requirements, Bangladesh maintains, can prevent resources from reaching communities when they are most urgently needed.
The issue has wider significance for developing countries as they seek to bridge the gap between the scale of climate action required and the financial support currently available.
Earlier, at COP29 in Baku, countries agreed that developed nations would take the lead in mobilizing at least $300 billion annually for developing countries by 2035, within a broader effort to scale up climate finance from all sources to $1.3 trillion a year by the same deadline. For Bangladesh and other vulnerable nations, the challenge is to ensure that such commitments translate into accessible funding, particularly for adaptation and loss and damage.
Bangladesh will seek greater accessibility and effectiveness of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, established to assist developing countries particularly vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change. Dhaka will advocate faster disbursement, simplified funding procedures and stronger support for communities facing irreversible climate impacts.
The country will also raise the importance of addressing non-economic losses, including displacement, disruption of traditional livelihoods and damage to cultural heritage and community identity. These concerns are particularly pressing for coastal and riverine communities in Bangladesh, where erosion, salinity intrusion, cyclones and other extreme weather events threaten homes, livelihoods and habitable land.
The government’s position is that international support must respond to the actual needs of affected populations rather than remain confined to financial pledges that are difficult to access. Bangladesh will therefore seek arrangements that allow vulnerable countries to respond to climate-related disasters while also investing in long-term resilience.
Bangladesh will call on countries to accelerate science-based greenhouse gas emission reductions in line with the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels.
Dhaka will urge developed countries to demonstrate leadership in cutting emissions and call on major emitting economies to strengthen their climate commitments in line with their responsibilities and respective capabilities. It will also emphasize that developing nations need finance, technology transfer and capacity-building support to implement their nationally determined contributions (NDCs).
For Bangladesh, stronger global mitigation is essential because adaptation alone cannot eliminate the growing risks associated with continued warming. The government will argue that the countries with the greatest historical responsibility and financial capacity must take the lead in reducing emissions while supporting vulnerable nations to pursue climate-resilient development.
Implementation of Bangladesh’s National Adaptation Plan (NAP) will be another major focus of the negotiations. The government will seek financial and technological assistance to strengthen resilience in coastal areas, wetlands, river islands and drought-prone regions.
Priority areas include water security, food production, public health, disaster preparedness and the protection of climate-sensitive livelihoods. Bangladesh will also highlight the importance of early warning systems, climate-resilient infrastructure and locally led adaptation initiatives.
Coastal communities facing cyclones and salinity intrusion, farmers affected by irregular rainfall and drought, and riverine populations confronting erosion and displacement are among those requiring stronger support. Dhaka will press for adaptation finance that reaches local communities and supports solutions shaped by their needs, traditional knowledge and direct experience of climate impacts.
Bangladesh will seek international cooperation to support a just and equitable transition towards low-carbon development across the energy, agriculture, industrial and transport sectors.
The government will emphasize that the costs and benefits of the transition must be distributed fairly, with particular attention to workers, low-income communities, women and young people. Skills development, social protection, labor rights and decent employment opportunities will be important elements of the country’s just transition agenda.
Dhaka will also advocate affordable access to renewable energy technologies, energy-efficient systems, cleaner industrial production and sustainable transport. Its position is that developing economies need international finance and technology to pursue cleaner growth without undermining employment, economic competitiveness or social development.
Bangladesh will explore opportunities to mobilize additional finance and technological support through international carbon markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. The mechanism allows countries to cooperate in meeting their climate commitments, including through internationally transferred emission reductions and other forms of cooperation.
Dhaka considers carbon markets a potential supplementary source of finance for implementing its NDCs and supporting low-carbon development. However, the government will maintain that carbon market cooperation cannot replace predictable public climate finance, particularly for adaptation and loss and damage.
Bangladesh will also seek stronger international cooperation on affordable climate technologies, technical expertise and institutional capacity-building. Such support will be important for renewable energy, climate-resilient agriculture, industrial decarbonization, water management and disaster preparedness.
The country will advocate greater international support for conserving forests, mangroves, wetlands and biodiversity as part of its wider climate response. Nature-based solutions can strengthen ecosystem resilience while supporting local livelihoods and sustainable resource management. They are particularly relevant to Bangladesh, where mangrove forests, wetlands and river systems provide protection against climate hazards and support millions of people.
Bangladesh will also emphasize inclusive climate governance and meaningful participation by women, children, young people, persons with disabilities and marginalized communities. The government will seek improved access to climate finance for women-led and locally led initiatives, arguing that climate policies must reflect the needs and experiences of vulnerable populations.
Bangladesh is also expected to raise concerns about climate-related international trade measures that could affect the exports, employment and competitiveness of developing economies.
Dhaka will seek cooperation to ensure that environmental trade policies do not place disproportionate burdens on countries with limited financial and technological capacity. The government will advocate assistance to help industries adopt cleaner technologies, improve energy efficiency and meet evolving international environmental standards.
Its position will be that the shift towards sustainable production should be supported through finance, technology transfer and capacity-building rather than measures that could undermine development opportunities. For Bangladesh, the challenge is to balance global climate objectives with economic growth, employment generation and poverty reduction.
Bangladesh will establish a 100-square-metre pavilion at the COP31 conference venue to showcase its climate vulnerabilities, adaptation experience and national priorities.
The pavilion will feature the country’s updated nationally determined contribution, known as NDC 3.0, alongside its National Adaptation Plan and initiatives addressing climate-induced loss and damage. Other areas of focus will include climate finance, renewable energy, carbon markets, nature-based solutions and technological innovations supporting climate resilience.
The pavilion is expected to provide a platform for policy discussions, knowledge exchange and engagement with international development partners, research institutions and potential investors. Bangladesh also intends to highlight locally developed adaptation solutions and community experiences, demonstrating how people directly affected by climate change are responding to its impacts.
The government hopes the pavilion will help create opportunities for partnerships, technical cooperation and investment aligned with national climate priorities.
Bangladesh’s negotiating position will be guided by equity and the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, a foundation of international climate cooperation. The principle recognizes that all countries have a role in addressing climate change, but their responsibilities and capacity to act differ according to historical circumstances and national capabilities.
Dhaka will argue that developed countries must fulfil their international commitments while providing vulnerable developing nations with the resources needed to implement climate action. The position also reflects a broader demand for accountability from major polluters, particularly as countries facing severe climate impacts struggle to finance adaptation and recovery.
For Bangladesh, climate justice is not limited to securing financial pledges. It also means ensuring that international support is accessible, reaches affected communities and reflects the scale of the damage they face.
COP31 comes at a critical point for international climate cooperation, with countries under growing pressure to turn existing commitments into measurable action.
Türkiye will host the conference, while Australia will chair the negotiations under the agreed organizational arrangement. Discussions are expected to focus on implementing the Paris Agreement, strengthening adaptation, mobilizing climate finance and supporting a fair transition towards cleaner energy systems.
With Prime Minister Tarique Rahman preparing to present the country’s position at the World Leaders’ Summit on November 11–12, Dhaka will seek to put grant-based finance, climate justice and the protection of vulnerable communities at the center of the discussions.
The success of COP31, from Bangladesh’s perspective, will ultimately depend not simply on new declarations but on whether international commitments deliver practical support to countries and communities already living with the consequences of climate change.

item.title: EC secretary: First phase of local polls to cover 1,050 union parishads
item.description:
The Election Commission (EC) plans to hold the first phase of the upcoming local government elections in 1,050 union parishads (UPs), Senior Secretary of the EC Secretariat Akhtar Ahmed said.
He disclosed the matter while speaking to reporters at the Election Commission headquarters in Agargaon, Dhaka, on Sunday.
Akhtar Ahmed said the commission is prioritising union parishads whose terms have expired and is preparing to hold elections in slightly more than 1,050 unions.
He also said the commission is considering collecting information for National Identity (NID) registration from children as young as six.
"We are discussing creating a database using the information provided when children enter primary school," he said.
The EC secretary said electronic voting machines (EVMs) would not be used in the upcoming elections.
The commission has begun a final stocktaking of the machines ahead of their disposal, he said, adding that the disposal method would be determined after receiving recommendations on the matter.

item.title: Riyadh financial district targeted, Aramco skyscraper damaged
item.description:
An Aramco building in Riyadh was targeted in an “attempted attack,” the Saudi energy ministry said on Sunday, with eyewitnesses telling AFP the skyscraper sustained damage, after the Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis said it had intercepted missiles launched by the group.
Aramco facilities and infrastructure have been repeatedly struck by the Houthis in recent months, with tankers, refineries, storage areas and the company headquarters all targeted by the group.
“Aramco tower in Kafd has been targeted, that’s the sure thing,” an eyewitness told AFP, referring to the King Abdullah Financial District. Two other witnesses confirmed seeing damage to the building.
A 2022 truce that had paused fighting in Yemen’s long-running conflict fell apart in July and Saudi Arabia has since traded blows with the Houthis, who have struck Saudi airports, energy infrastructure and military sites.
The Iran-backed Houthis seized the Yemeni capital Sanaa in 2014, with the Saudi-led coalition entering the conflict a year later in support of the government.
One eyewitness in the area of the Aramco skyscraper told AFP they saw a projectile strike the building but they were unsure what type of projectile it was.
The King Abdullah Financial District is one of the most visible manifestations of the kingdom’s ongoing economic and social reforms drive, with towering glass skyscrapers, high-end retail outlets and green spaces dotting the area.
Kafd is home to some of the kingdom’s biggest home-grown companies and blue-chip international firms like Goldman Sachs.
The headquarters of the kingdom’s influential sovereign wealth fund -- the Public Investment Fund -- and the Saudi stock exchange are also located in the heart of the district.
Targeting the area, which is also home to residential housing and a large metro station with heavy commuter traffic during the morning rush hour, would mark a major escalation in the kingdom’s fight with the Houthis.
Multiple floors of the Aramco tower appeared to have sustained damage, said another witness, with glass shattered and damage to part of the tower’s facade visible.
The energy ministry said in a statement that “an administrative building belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh was subjected to an attempted attack today”.
“The incident resulted in falling shrapnel that caused minor damage to the building, with no injuries or fatalities reported, thankfully.”
AFP was unable to confirm the extent of the damage.
The kingdom’s interior ministry has repeatedly warned residents against filming and publishing images of drones, missiles, air defense interceptors and the impacts of barrages.
The attack comes hours after the kingdom’s education ministry announced, late on Saturday, the return of in-person schooling after weeks of remote-learning in Riyadh following an earlier wave of strikes.
Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki, in a Sunday morning social media post, said that “air defenses intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthi terrorist militia towards Riyadh”, as loud explosions were heard in the Saudi capital.
The kingdom has been pressing allies for help as it comes under daily fire from the Houthis that recently seized swathes of the Red Sea coastline from the Riyadh-backed government.
Thousands of Syrian troops are set to deploy to Saudi Arabia and Yemen, with some already on the ground, multiple Yemeni officials told AFP.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed in impoverished Yemen.
The fragile 2022 truce fell apart after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen’s capital Sanaa in defiance of Saudi control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
Later, the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before seizing Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast in a lightning campaign.
